content.intro: This lesson develops topic 85 of the supplied curriculum: **Common Broadcasting Errors**. The main starting point is **Incompatible shapes**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Broadcasting allows compatible shapes to operate without explicitly copying repeated values. Reason about the dimensions from the rightmost side before changing the arrays.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Common Broadcasting Errors** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Incompatible shapes** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.title: Subtopics from the supplied curriculum
items: A repeatable method for debugging shapes

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 4))
print('incompatible shapes:', a.shape, b.shape)
content_blocks.expected_output:
Observed output in the available validation environment (Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5):
incompatible shapes: (2, 3) (2, 4)

common_mistakes.why: Broadcasting compares dimensions from the right.
common_mistakes.fix: Write the shapes side by side and align their rightmost dimensions.

common_mistakes.why: Explicit tiling can allocate extra memory.
common_mistakes.fix: Try broadcasting with singleton dimensions first.
